source_name: Greenhawt & Fleischer — Primary Prevention of Food Allergy (Curr Allergy Asthma Rep 2017)
text: Food allergy affects roughly 8% of children in the USA, has no established cure, and ranges from mild to life-threatening in severity.

source_name: Greenhawt & Fleischer — Primary Prevention of Food Allergy (Curr Allergy Asthma Rep 2017)
text: In the LEAP trial, infants at high risk (severe eczema and/or egg allergy) who consumed 2g of peanut protein three times weekly from 4-11 months through age 5 had an 80% relative risk reduction and 17-percentage-point absolute risk reduction in peanut allergy compared with infants who avoided peanut for 5 years.

source_name: Greenhawt & Fleischer — Primary Prevention of Food Allergy (Curr Allergy Asthma Rep 2017)
text: On intention-to-treat analysis, 13.7% of children in the peanut-avoidance arm developed challenge-confirmed peanut allergy by age 5, versus 1.9% in the peanut-consumption arm; this benefit held in both children with minimal peanut sensitization (1-4mm wheal) and non-sensitized children.

source_name: Greenhawt & Fleischer — Primary Prevention of Food Allergy (Curr Allergy Asthma Rep 2017)
text: The 2017 NIAID addendum defines three risk tiers: (1) severe eczema and/or egg allergy — strongly consider sIgE/skin-prick testing and possibly an oral food challenge before introducing peanut; (2) mild-to-moderate eczema — introduce peanut-containing foods at home around 6 months; (3) no eczema or food allergy — introduce peanut in an age-appropriate way per family/cultural preference.

source_name: Greenhawt & Fleischer — Primary Prevention of Food Allergy (Curr Allergy Asthma Rep 2017)
text: Under the NIAID addendum, a peanut skin-prick wheal of 0-2mm supports home introduction; 3-7mm supports an in-office supervised feeding or graded challenge; 8mm or larger is treated as probable allergy, and the infant should be managed as allergic, though in-office introduction can still be considered if the family and provider agree.

source_name: Greenhawt & Fleischer — Primary Prevention of Food Allergy (Curr Allergy Asthma Rep 2017)
text: The dose used across the LEAP protocol and NIAID addendum for prevention is 2g of peanut protein at least three times a week, for example one heaped teaspoon of diluted peanut butter per serving; peanut should not be the first solid food introduced, to avoid mistaking normal early feeding symptoms for an allergic reaction.

source_name: Greenhawt & Fleischer — Primary Prevention of Food Allergy (Curr Allergy Asthma Rep 2017)
text: In the EAT study, standard-risk exclusively breastfed infants were randomized to early introduction (from 3 months) versus standard introduction (around 6 months) of six allergens. Intention-to-treat analysis showed no significant overall difference in food allergy, but the per-protocol analysis (infants who actually adhered) showed significantly less peanut allergy (absolute risk reduction 2.5%) and egg allergy (absolute risk reduction 4.1%) in the early-introduction group.

source_name: Greenhawt & Fleischer — Primary Prevention of Food Allergy (Curr Allergy Asthma Rep 2017)
text: The STAR trial gave raw pasteurized egg powder from 4 months to eczema-affected infants but was stopped prematurely: about a third of the 4-month-old participants were already both egg-sensitized and reactive to egg at trial entry, suggesting some infants were sensitized before the trial even started. The trend favored egg introduction (33% vs 51% egg allergy at 12 months) but did not reach statistical significance.

source_name: Greenhawt & Fleischer — Primary Prevention of Food Allergy (Curr Allergy Asthma Rep 2017)
text: The STEP trial, in infants of atopic mothers without pre-existing eczema, found a non-significant 3.3% absolute risk reduction in egg allergy at 12 months favoring earlier egg introduction (4-6.5 months vs 10 months), alongside significant drops in egg-specific IgE and rises in egg IgG4.

source_name: Greenhawt & Fleischer — Primary Prevention of Food Allergy (Curr Allergy Asthma Rep 2017)
text: The BEAT trial found no significant difference in egg allergy at 12 months between early (4 months) and later (8 months) egg introduction, but did find a significant 9.7 percentage-point reduction in egg sensitization favoring earlier introduction; some non-sensitized infants had mild-to-moderate reactions in the first week.

source_name: Greenhawt & Fleischer — Primary Prevention of Food Allergy (Curr Allergy Asthma Rep 2017)
text: The German HEAP trial found no significant reduction in egg sensitization or allergy with thrice-weekly raw pasteurized egg from 4-6 months, and three of twelve already egg-sensitized infants in the intervention arm had severe reactions on first exposure — evidence against introducing egg this way without prior screening in that population.

source_name: Greenhawt & Fleischer — Primary Prevention of Food Allergy (Curr Allergy Asthma Rep 2017)
text: The Japanese PETIT trial used a two-step protocol: 50mg/day heated egg powder from 6-9 months, increasing to 250mg/day from 9-12 months, in infants with eczema whose eczema was actively treated first. Egg allergy developed in 9% of the egg group versus 38% of placebo, a large enough effect that the trial was stopped early on ethical grounds.

source_name: Greenhawt & Fleischer — Primary Prevention of Food Allergy (Curr Allergy Asthma Rep 2017)
text: A 2016 meta-analysis (Ierodiakonou et al.) found moderate-certainty evidence that peanut introduced between 4-11 months reduces peanut allergy risk, and moderate-certainty evidence that egg introduced between 4-6 months reduces egg allergy risk, but cautioned that trial-sequential analysis suggested thousands more participants would be needed for high-certainty conclusions on egg, and that real-world generalizability of the pooled results was uncertain.

source_name: Greenhawt & Fleischer — Primary Prevention of Food Allergy (Curr Allergy Asthma Rep 2017)
text: As of this 2017 review, no formal national guideline had yet recommended early egg introduction specifically to prevent egg allergy, even though the pooled trial evidence pointed that way — this was flagged as a gap between the peanut and egg evidence bases at the time.

source_name: Greenhawt & Fleischer — Primary Prevention of Food Allergy (Curr Allergy Asthma Rep 2017)
text: Real-world experience from Israel and Australia, where early peanut introduction is recommended for all infants without routine pre-screening, suggests at-home introduction is safe in practice; the article questions whether mandatory in-office pre-evaluation is truly necessary or driven more by clinician caution than by demonstrated need.

source_name: Greenhawt & Fleischer — Primary Prevention of Food Allergy (Curr Allergy Asthma Rep 2017)
text: At the time of this review there were fewer than 5700 allergists in the US and Canada combined, and fewer than 20% of them regularly performed oral food challenges — a practical bottleneck if guidelines require in-office supervised introduction for all higher-risk infants.

source_name: Greenhawt & Fleischer — Primary Prevention of Food Allergy (Curr Allergy Asthma Rep 2017)
text: Practical guidance for home introduction of peanut: don't make it the first solid food; only try it when the baby is otherwise well (no concurrent illness); introduce for the first time at home, not at daycare or a restaurant; have one caregiver able to give full attention; give a small taste, wait about 10 minutes, then give the rest if tolerated; allow up to 2 hours to watch for a reaction; avoid whole peanuts or peanut butter straight off a spoon before age 4 due to choking risk.

source_name: Greenhawt & Fleischer — Primary Prevention of Food Allergy (Curr Allergy Asthma Rep 2017)
text: The NIAID addendum's high-risk category is based on the infant's own severe eczema and/or egg allergy — not simply a first-degree relative having any allergic disease. A family history of allergy alone was not treated as a high-risk criterion in the LEAP study or the addendum.

source_name: Greenhawt & Fleischer — Primary Prevention of Food Allergy (Curr Allergy Asthma Rep 2017)
text: There is some debate about whether food allergy prevalence is truly rising: US self-reported survey data suggest an increase, but the trend is less clear in other countries, and re-analysis of a repeated UK cohort (Isle of Wight, surveyed 12 years apart) has questioned whether peanut allergy prevalence has genuinely risen as much as assumed.

source_name: Greenhawt & Fleischer — Primary Prevention of Food Allergy (Curr Allergy Asthma Rep 2017)
text: At the time of this review, two food-targeted oral immunotherapy products for treating (not preventing) existing food allergy were in phase III trials — a reminder that early-introduction prevention strategies and immunotherapy treatment strategies are separate approaches addressing different points in the allergy timeline.

source_name: Greenhawt & Fleischer — Primary Prevention of Food Allergy (Curr Allergy Asthma Rep 2017)
text: The PETIT trial's effect size translated to a number needed to treat of about 3.4, meaning roughly one case of egg allergy was prevented for every 3-4 high-risk eczema infants given the early, staged egg introduction protocol.

source_name: Greenhawt & Fleischer — Primary Prevention of Food Allergy (Curr Allergy Asthma Rep 2017)
text: The EAT study's early-introduction protocol offered six allergenic foods — peanut, cooked egg, cow's milk, sesame, whitefish, and wheat — to exclusively breastfed infants from around 3 months, each given twice weekly at roughly 2g of protein per food, alongside continued breastfeeding.

source_name: Tham et al. — APAPARI Consensus: Early Allergenic Food Introduction, Asian Perspective (Pediatr Allergy Immunol 2018)
guidance_status: current (APAPARI regional adaptation of Western guidance)
text: APAPARI notes that Western guidelines (US NIAID addendum, European consensus) focus mainly on preventing peanut allergy, but peanut allergy prevalence is low across most of Asia (with the exception of Japan); the consensus argues these Western guidelines cannot simply be transplanted onto Asian populations without adaptation.

source_name: Tham et al. — APAPARI Consensus: Early Allergenic Food Introduction, Asian Perspective (Pediatr Allergy Immunol 2018)
guidance_status: current (APAPARI regional adaptation of Western guidance)
text: Food allergy prevalence in Asia follows a rough latitude gradient: higher in northern countries such as Japan (5-10%) and Korea (5.3%), and lower (under 5%) in Hong Kong, China, the Philippines, and Singapore.

source_name: Tham et al. — APAPARI Consensus: Early Allergenic Food Introduction, Asian Perspective (Pediatr Allergy Immunol 2018)
guidance_status: current (APAPARI regional adaptation of Western guidance)
text: Unlike Western countries, wheat is among the most common food allergens (after egg and milk) in Thailand and Japan, and shellfish allergy is common in late childhood and adolescence in Singapore and the Philippines; peanut allergy is relatively uncommon across most of Asia except Japan.

source_name: Tham et al. — APAPARI Consensus: Early Allergenic Food Introduction, Asian Perspective (Pediatr Allergy Immunol 2018)
guidance_status: current (APAPARI regional adaptation of Western guidance)
text: Because egg is the most common infant food allergen across most Asian countries and peanut allergy prevalence is low outside Japan, APAPARI's dietary-deviation recommendations focus specifically on egg prevention in high-risk infants, with peanut screening/introduction reserved for countries where peanut allergy prevalence is high.

source_name: Tham et al. — APAPARI Consensus: Early Allergenic Food Introduction, Asian Perspective (Pediatr Allergy Immunol 2018)
guidance_status: current (APAPARI regional adaptation of Western guidance)
text: For healthy infants with no risk factors, APAPARI recommends no change to standard feeding guidelines: follow WHO guidance to introduce complementary foods around 6 months, with breastfeeding continuing alongside complementary feeding up to 2 years where possible, according to each country's cultural practices.

source_name: Tham et al. — APAPARI Consensus: Early Allergenic Food Introduction, Asian Perspective (Pediatr Allergy Immunol 2018)
guidance_status: current (APAPARI regional adaptation of Western guidance)
text: For infants with non-severe eczema or a family history of atopy (but not severe eczema), APAPARI recommends no delay in introducing allergenic foods, including egg, cow's milk, peanut, soy, wheat, and shellfish, introduced sensibly once weaning has begun.

source_name: Tham et al. — APAPARI Consensus: Early Allergenic Food Introduction, Asian Perspective (Pediatr Allergy Immunol 2018)
guidance_status: current (APAPARI regional adaptation of Western guidance)
text: For infants with severe eczema (high risk), APAPARI recommends beginning clinical evaluation (history, skin-prick and/or specific IgE testing, focused on egg and peanut where peanut prevalence is high) from 4 months of age but ideally not later than 10 months, in countries with ready access to allergy expertise, followed by supervised oral food challenge if sensitized.

source_name: Tham et al. — APAPARI Consensus: Early Allergenic Food Introduction, Asian Perspective (Pediatr Allergy Immunol 2018)
guidance_status: current (APAPARI regional adaptation of Western guidance)
text: In countries with limited access to allergy expertise, APAPARI recommends that families who want early introduction for a severely eczematous infant have careful oral food challenges performed in the office of a doctor trained in recognizing and managing allergic reactions, rather than skipping supervision altogether.

source_name: Tham et al. — APAPARI Consensus: Early Allergenic Food Introduction, Asian Perspective (Pediatr Allergy Immunol 2018)
guidance_status: current (APAPARI regional adaptation of Western guidance)
text: APAPARI defines severe eczema as a persistent or frequently recurring rash with typical eczema features and distribution, assessed as severe by a healthcare provider, that has required topical corticosteroids or calcineurin inhibitors despite proper use of emollients.

source_name: Tham et al. — APAPARI Consensus: Early Allergenic Food Introduction, Asian Perspective (Pediatr Allergy Immunol 2018)
guidance_status: current (APAPARI regional adaptation of Western guidance)
text: The Australian HealthNuts study found peanut and egg allergy rates were about three times higher in Australian-born infants of Asian-born parents compared with infants of parents born in the UK or Europe; a related study found a similar threefold higher risk of parent-reported peanut allergy in Australian-born children of Asian mothers versus Australian-born white children, while birth in Asia followed by migration to Australia appeared protective against nut allergy.

source_name: Tham et al. — APAPARI Consensus: Early Allergenic Food Introduction, Asian Perspective (Pediatr Allergy Immunol 2018)
guidance_status: current (APAPARI regional adaptation of Western guidance)
text: The Singaporean GUSTO cohort found very low food allergy prevalence (peaking at only 2.9% at 12 months) despite late introduction of egg, peanut, and shellfish (after 10 months of age), with no significant association found between delayed introduction and food allergy, even in the subgroup with eczema.

source_name: Tham et al. — APAPARI Consensus: Early Allergenic Food Introduction, Asian Perspective (Pediatr Allergy Immunol 2018)
guidance_status: current (APAPARI regional adaptation of Western guidance)
text: APAPARI's authors note there is a paucity of Asia-specific data on the association between timing of allergenic food introduction and food allergy development, and that existing regional studies show conflicting results; most predictive thresholds for skin-prick tests and specific IgE used in practice are extrapolated from non-Asian populations.

source_name: Tham et al. — APAPARI Consensus: Early Allergenic Food Introduction, Asian Perspective (Pediatr Allergy Immunol 2018)
guidance_status: current (APAPARI regional adaptation of Western guidance)
text: The PETIT trial (Natsume et al.) was, at the time of this consensus, the first randomized controlled trial conducted within Asia specifically testing early heated-egg introduction in high-risk infants with eczema, and found a significantly reduced risk of hen's egg allergy at 12 months in the intervention group versus placebo.

source_name: Tham et al. — APAPARI Consensus: Early Allergenic Food Introduction, Asian Perspective (Pediatr Allergy Immunol 2018)
guidance_status: current (APAPARI regional adaptation of Western guidance)
text: APAPARI recommends peanut be screened for, alongside egg, only in high-risk infants living in countries where peanut allergy prevalence is high; in countries with low peanut prevalence, peanut screening is not part of the recommended high-risk pathway.

source_name: Tham et al. — APAPARI Consensus: Early Allergenic Food Introduction, Asian Perspective (Pediatr Allergy Immunol 2018)
guidance_status: current (APAPARI regional adaptation of Western guidance)
text: Studies establishing 95% positive predictive values for skin-prick test and specific IgE thresholds have mostly been carried out in non-Asian populations. There are currently no validated population-based predictive thresholds for challenge-proven food allergy in Asian infants, so sensitization cutoffs are set by each clinical center's own practice.

source_name: Tham et al. — APAPARI Consensus: Early Allergenic Food Introduction, Asian Perspective (Pediatr Allergy Immunol 2018)
guidance_status: current (APAPARI regional adaptation of Western guidance)
text: Once an infant sensitized to egg or peanut passes a supervised oral food challenge, APAPARI recommends the allergenic food be introduced into the infant's regular diet as soon as possible afterward, rather than delayed further.

source_name: Tham et al. — APAPARI Consensus: Early Allergenic Food Introduction, Asian Perspective (Pediatr Allergy Immunol 2018)
guidance_status: current (APAPARI regional adaptation of Western guidance)
text: The dual-allergen exposure hypothesis proposes that food sensitization can occur through a disrupted skin barrier (as in eczema) in early life, while early oral exposure to the same food instead promotes tolerance — part of the mechanistic rationale for pairing skin care with early food introduction in high-risk infants.

source_name: Tham et al. — APAPARI Consensus: Early Allergenic Food Introduction, Asian Perspective (Pediatr Allergy Immunol 2018)
guidance_status: current (APAPARI regional adaptation of Western guidance)
text: An outbreak of wheat allergy occurred in Japan among users of a facial soap containing hydrolyzed wheat protein, illustrating that allergen exposure through the skin (not only diet) can drive sensitization — relevant context for why skin-barrier care matters alongside dietary introduction.

source_name: Tham et al. — APAPARI Consensus: Early Allergenic Food Introduction, Asian Perspective (Pediatr Allergy Immunol 2018)
guidance_status: current (APAPARI regional adaptation of Western guidance)
text: If an infant is sensitized and does not pass a supervised oral food challenge, that specific food is avoided in the regular diet for the time being, and the family is guided to re-evaluate later with their allergy provider rather than treating the result as a permanent restriction.

source_name: Tham et al. — APAPARI Consensus: Early Allergenic Food Introduction, Asian Perspective (Pediatr Allergy Immunol 2018)
guidance_status: current (APAPARI regional adaptation of Western guidance)
text: Infant weaning practice surveys show most infants in China, Hong Kong and Japan start solids before 6 months, some even before 4 months, while most infants in Singapore and Taiwan start after 4-6 months; these surveys did not specifically analyze high-risk subgroups such as infants with eczema.

source_name: Klain et al. — SIAIP Position Paper: PUFAs in Primary Prevention of Allergic Disease (Nutrients 2026)
text: In the COPSAC2010 trial, 736 pregnant women were randomized at 24 weeks' gestation to 2.4g/day of EPA+DHA or placebo (olive oil) until one week postpartum. Persistent wheeze or asthma occurred in 16.9% of the supplementation group versus 23.7% of controls (hazard ratio 0.69), a roughly 30% relative risk reduction sustained to 5 years of follow-up; the effect was larger in mothers who started with low baseline EPA/DHA levels.

source_name: Klain et al. — SIAIP Position Paper: PUFAs in Primary Prevention of Allergic Disease (Nutrients 2026)
text: In the same COPSAC2010 trial, omega-3 supplementation was also linked to fewer lower respiratory tract infections, but no significant effect was found on allergic sensitization or eczema.

source_name: Klain et al. — SIAIP Position Paper: PUFAs in Primary Prevention of Allergic Disease (Nutrients 2026)
text: A dose-response meta-analysis of 3037 mother-infant pairs found prenatal long-chain omega-3 supplementation did not significantly reduce asthma/wheeze risk overall, but did show significant protection at doses of 1200mg/day or higher, and when supplementation continued from pregnancy into lactation; each extra 100mg/day of intake was linked to about a 2% further reduction in risk.

source_name: Klain et al. — SIAIP Position Paper: PUFAs in Primary Prevention of Allergic Disease (Nutrients 2026)
text: In the DOMInO trial, 900mg/day of omega-3 long-chain PUFAs (800mg DHA + 100mg EPA) from 21 weeks' gestation did not significantly reduce overall IgE-mediated allergic disease at 1 or 3 years, though a reduction in atopic eczema and egg sensitization was seen at 1 year in that trial.

source_name: Klain et al. — SIAIP Position Paper: PUFAs in Primary Prevention of Allergic Disease (Nutrients 2026)
text: A Cochrane systematic review of 8 RCTs (3366 women, 3175 children) found maternal long-chain omega-3 supplementation during pregnancy and/or lactation was linked to a significant reduction in IgE-mediated allergic disease at 12-36 months, but this benefit was not sustained beyond 36 months, and no consistent reduction was found for asthma or wheeze specifically.

source_name: Klain et al. — SIAIP Position Paper: PUFAs in Primary Prevention of Allergic Disease (Nutrients 2026)
text: A meta-analysis of 13 cohort studies plus one RCT found that dietary fish intake during the first year of life (not supplementation) was linked to a significant reduction in eczema and allergic rhinitis, while maternal fish intake during pregnancy specifically was not linked to reduced allergic outcomes in that analysis.

source_name: Klain et al. — SIAIP Position Paper: PUFAs in Primary Prevention of Allergic Disease (Nutrients 2026)
text: EFSA dietary reference values recommend a minimum DHA intake of 100mg/day from around 7 months of age, maintained at 100mg/day up to age 2, with combined EPA+DHA of 250mg/day recommended thereafter; pregnant and lactating women are advised 250mg/day EPA+DHA plus an additional 100-200mg/day of DHA to support fetal and neonatal development.

source_name: Klain et al. — SIAIP Position Paper: PUFAs in Primary Prevention of Allergic Disease (Nutrients 2026)
text: The SIAIP position statement suggests that when dietary omega-3 intake is inadequate, targeted supplementation providing roughly 2g/day of combined EPA and DHA may be considered as part of a preventive nutritional strategy, particularly for women with low omega-3 status or increased hereditary allergy risk, and under clinical supervision.

source_name: Klain et al. — SIAIP Position Paper: PUFAs in Primary Prevention of Allergic Disease (Nutrients 2026)
text: Modern Western diets tend to have an excess of omega-6 relative to omega-3 fatty acids, a pattern linked to a more pro-inflammatory state; higher omega-6 PUFA intake has been associated with increased odds of allergic rhinitis in a large NHANES analysis, while higher omega-3 intake showed no such adverse association.

source_name: Klain et al. — SIAIP Position Paper: PUFAs in Primary Prevention of Allergic Disease (Nutrients 2026)
text: Wild fatty fish naturally contain a higher omega-3-to-omega-6 ratio than farmed fish, because farmed fish are often fed terrestrial vegetable oils; however, wild fish tend to have somewhat higher levels of certain environmental contaminants (dioxins, PCBs, mercury) due to bioaccumulation, though both wild and farmed salmon generally remain below current EU safety limits for these contaminants.

source_name: Klain et al. — SIAIP Position Paper: PUFAs in Primary Prevention of Allergic Disease (Nutrients 2026)
text: Marine sources such as salmon, herring, sardines, mackerel, and trout are rich in the biologically active long-chain omega-3s EPA and DHA; plant sources like flaxseed, chia seeds, and walnuts provide ALA, which the body converts to EPA/DHA very inefficiently (roughly 2-5% conversion), so plant sources alone are unlikely to reach the same EPA/DHA levels as marine sources.

source_name: Klain et al. — SIAIP Position Paper: PUFAs in Primary Prevention of Allergic Disease (Nutrients 2026)
text: Across the studies reviewed, long-chain omega-3 supplementation in the 2-3g/day range was generally well tolerated in healthy pregnant and lactating women, with no consistent evidence of significant adverse effects reported at these doses; individual clinical judgment is still advised.

source_name: Klain et al. — SIAIP Position Paper: PUFAs in Primary Prevention of Allergic Disease (Nutrients 2026)
text: In the Project Viva cohort, higher maternal plasma EPA in the second trimester was linked to lower allergic sensitization and current asthma in mid-childhood, but higher maternal fish/shellfish intake was, unexpectedly, associated with increased allergic sensitization risk in the same cohort — a reminder that whole-food fish intake and purified EPA/DHA exposure don't always behave identically in observational data.

source_name: Klain et al. — SIAIP Position Paper: PUFAs in Primary Prevention of Allergic Disease (Nutrients 2026)
text: In pooled analyses, the protective effect of prenatal omega-3 on respiratory outcomes appears more consistent in women with low baseline omega-3 status or in offspring at increased hereditary allergic risk, rather than as a universal effect across all pregnancies.

source_name: Klain et al. — SIAIP Position Paper: PUFAs in Primary Prevention of Allergic Disease (Nutrients 2026)
text: This position paper addresses maternal/infant omega-3 fatty acid intake as one nutritional strategy within a broader multifactorial prevention approach; it does not substitute for, and is discussed separately from, the timing of solid-food and allergen introduction covered by other guidelines.

source_name: Klain et al. — SIAIP Position Paper: PUFAs in Primary Prevention of Allergic Disease (Nutrients 2026)
text: Not all commercial 'omega-3' or fish oil supplements are equivalent: EPA/DHA concentration, purity, oxidation status, and contaminant screening vary widely between products, so the position paper advises checking the actual EPA+DHA content per dose rather than relying on total fish oil volume stated on the label.

source_name: Klain et al. — SIAIP Position Paper: PUFAs in Primary Prevention of Allergic Disease (Nutrients 2026)
text: Algae-derived omega-3 products are highlighted as a valuable option for vegetarian or vegan individuals seeking adequate EPA/DHA intake, since plant sources such as flaxseed and chia provide only ALA, which the body converts to EPA/DHA very inefficiently.

source_name: Klain et al. — SIAIP Position Paper: PUFAs in Primary Prevention of Allergic Disease (Nutrients 2026)
text: Common cooking methods such as baking, frying, and boiling generally preserve a substantial share of a fish's EPA+DHA content, though the exact amount retained varies by fish species and preparation method.

source_name: Klain et al. — SIAIP Position Paper: PUFAs in Primary Prevention of Allergic Disease (Nutrients 2026)
text: Docosapentaenoic acid (DPA), an intermediate between EPA and DHA, is present in marine foods and immune-cell membranes and is biologically plausible as another active omega-3, but has been far less studied than EPA/DHA in pediatric allergy prevention, so it does not yet support specific clinical recommendations on its own.

source_name: Klain et al. — SIAIP Position Paper: PUFAs in Primary Prevention of Allergic Disease (Nutrients 2026)
text: The position paper frames omega-3 supplementation as one part of a broader allergy-prevention approach that also includes avoiding tobacco smoke exposure, promoting breastfeeding where possible, and timely introduction of complementary/allergenic foods — not a standalone substitute for those other measures.

source_name: Shakhova et al. — Evolution of Approaches to Primary Prevention of Food Allergy: Elimination to Early Introduction (Current Pediatrics 2025)
text: Large systematic reviews and meta-analyses (Kramer & Kakuma 2012; Garcia-Larsen et al. 2018) found no protective effect of maternal elimination diets during pregnancy or breastfeeding against atopic dermatitis or food allergy in the child, and major bodies (EAACI, AAAAI/ACAAI/CSACI, AAP, and Russian pediatric societies) uniformly advise against hypoallergenic or elimination diets in pregnant/breastfeeding women for allergy prevention.

source_name: Shakhova et al. — Evolution of Approaches to Primary Prevention of Food Allergy: Elimination to Early Introduction (Current Pediatrics 2025)
text: A 2021 study (Azad et al.) found that maternal peanut consumption during pregnancy, combined with early peanut introduction to the infant while breastfeeding, was associated with a large reduction in infant peanut sensitization (odds ratio 0.07).

source_name: Shakhova et al. — Evolution of Approaches to Primary Prevention of Food Allergy: Elimination to Early Introduction (Current Pediatrics 2025)
text: A Swedish cohort study (Bodén et al. 2023) found that high dietary diversity in the mother's pregnancy diet was associated with a 43% lower risk of food allergy in children by age 7; Singaporean GUSTO/S-PRESTO cohort data similarly linked maternal diets rich in omega-3s and legumes with reduced sensitization risk.

source_name: Shakhova et al. — Evolution of Approaches to Primary Prevention of Food Allergy: Elimination to Early Introduction (Current Pediatrics 2025)
text: Evidence on breastfeeding's effect on food allergy specifically is inconsistent: an early meta-analysis (Lodge et al. 2015) found no significant association; a large Japanese cohort (Matsumoto et al. 2020, n=46,616) found partial breastfeeding including only colostrum lowered risk in infants with eczema but exclusive breastfeeding raised risk in infants without eczema; a 2024 meta-analysis (Ding et al.) found no overall association by feeding type but a U-shaped relationship with duration, where breastfeeding beyond 6 months was linked to increased food allergy risk, possibly reflecting later introduction of solids in longer-breastfed infants.

source_name: Shakhova et al. — Evolution of Approaches to Primary Prevention of Food Allergy: Elimination to Early Introduction (Current Pediatrics 2025)
text: A 2024 meta-analysis (Wang et al., 12 studies, 14,439 children) found early introduction of allergenic foods reduced food allergy risk overall (odds ratio 0.62), with an even larger reduction when allergens were introduced at 10-12 months compared with introduction after 12 months (odds ratio 0.13); the effect held for both high-risk and general-population infants.

source_name: Shakhova et al. — Evolution of Approaches to Primary Prevention of Food Allergy: Elimination to Early Introduction (Current Pediatrics 2025)
text: Evidence on cow's milk formula timing is mixed: a Japanese study (Sakihara et al. 2021) found adding a small amount of cow's-milk-based formula around 2 months of age significantly reduced later cow's milk allergy in breastfed infants, whereas the ABS trial (Urashima et al. 2019) found introducing unmodified cow's-milk-protein formula within the first 3 days of life increased the risk of cow's milk allergy compared with an amino-acid formula — suggesting a possible 'window of tolerance' that opens somewhat later than the immediate newborn period.

source_name: Shakhova et al. — Evolution of Approaches to Primary Prevention of Food Allergy: Elimination to Early Introduction (Current Pediatrics 2025)
text: A 2016 meta-analysis (Boyle et al.) pooling partially hydrolyzed formulas from different manufacturers found no significant overall reduction in food allergy risk, leading several bodies (AAAAI, ASCIA, Japanese pediatric guidelines) to stop recommending partially hydrolyzed formula generally for allergy prevention; however, the authors of this review argue that pooling different formulas together is methodologically flawed, since hydrolysis degree, protein source and peptide profile differ by product, and that evidence should be assessed per specific formula rather than as a class — noting one specific product (a partially hydrolyzed whey formula) with a larger evidence base, including a 20-year follow-up (the GINI study), showing reduced atopic dermatitis and other allergic outcomes.

source_name: Shakhova et al. — Evolution of Approaches to Primary Prevention of Food Allergy: Elimination to Early Introduction (Current Pediatrics 2025)
text: Consumption of food allergens by a breastfeeding mother is associated with detectable allergen traces in her breast milk and with higher levels of allergen-specific IgG4 (a marker linked to oral tolerance induction) in her infant, one proposed mechanism by which maternal diet during lactation could support tolerance rather than sensitization.

source_name: Shakhova et al. — Evolution of Approaches to Primary Prevention of Food Allergy: Elimination to Early Introduction (Current Pediatrics 2025)
text: The Union of Pediatricians of Russia's draft clinical guidelines, aligned with EAACI, AAAAI/ACAAI/CSACI and AAP, do not recommend hypoallergenic or elimination diets during pregnancy or breastfeeding, but — differing somewhat from EAACI/AAAAI/AAP, which decline to credit breastfeeding specifically with preventing food allergy — the Russian guidelines do recommend breastfeeding as a food-allergy prevention measure, citing exclusive breastfeeding to 4-6 months as having a meaningful protective effect in the evidence they reviewed.

source_name: Shakhova et al. — Evolution of Approaches to Primary Prevention of Food Allergy: Elimination to Early Introduction (Current Pediatrics 2025)
text: The review concludes that early introduction of allergenic foods around 4-6 months has become the most consistently supported strategy across recent international guidelines, replacing the older elimination-based paradigm, and that this shift is reflected in current Russian pediatric guidance as well.

source_name: Shakhova et al. — Evolution of Approaches to Primary Prevention of Food Allergy: Elimination to Early Introduction (Current Pediatrics 2025)
text: The authors argue that pooled meta-analyses of hydrolyzed formulas are limited by combining products that differ in protein source, degree of hydrolysis, and peptide profile under one umbrella, and that a 'hypoallergenic' label alone is not sufficient evidence of a preventive effect — each specific formula needs its own supporting clinical trial data confirming reduced allergy risk, ideally with long-term follow-up.

source_name: Shakhova et al. — Evolution of Approaches to Primary Prevention of Food Allergy: Elimination to Early Introduction (Current Pediatrics 2025)
text: Because no benefit from maternal elimination diets has been demonstrated, and such diets carry a real risk of nutrient deficiency for the mother, international and Russian guidelines consistently advise against them rather than treating them as a low-risk precaution.

source_name: Shakhova et al. — Evolution of Approaches to Primary Prevention of Food Allergy: Elimination to Early Introduction (Current Pediatrics 2025)
text: Food allergens from a mother's diet — cow's milk, egg, wheat, peanut and others — have been detected in breast milk in very small amounts, both free and bound to IgA/IgG antibodies; this is part of the proposed mechanism for how maternal diet during breastfeeding may influence infant tolerance, alongside transfer of immune factors like secretory IgA, TGF-beta, and IL-10.

source_name: Shakhova et al. — Evolution of Approaches to Primary Prevention of Food Allergy: Elimination to Early Introduction (Current Pediatrics 2025)
text: This review did not identify direct evidence comparing the ideal timing of allergenic-solid introduction between exclusively breastfed and formula-fed infants specifically; general age-based introduction guidance (around 4-6 months) is presented without a feeding-type-specific adjustment.

source_name: Shakhova et al. — Evolution of Approaches to Primary Prevention of Food Allergy: Elimination to Early Introduction (Current Pediatrics 2025)
text: The GINI study followed children given one specific partially hydrolyzed whey formula for up to 20 years and found reduced rates of atopic dermatitis, among other allergic outcomes — offered as an example of the kind of product-specific, long-term evidence the authors argue should be required before crediting any hydrolyzed formula with a preventive effect.

source_name: Shakhova et al. — Evolution of Approaches to Primary Prevention of Food Allergy: Elimination to Early Introduction (Current Pediatrics 2025)
text: Weighing the overall evidence base, the strongest and most consistent support across guidelines is for early introduction of allergenic solids around 4-6 months; evidence for breastfeeding's specific anti-allergy effect and for hydrolyzed formulas remains inconsistent and product/context dependent by comparison.

source_name: Shakhova et al. — Evolution of Approaches to Primary Prevention of Food Allergy: Elimination to Early Introduction (Current Pediatrics 2025)
text: Food allergens have also been shown to cross the placenta during pregnancy, part of the historical rationale for maternal elimination diets that later trials failed to support as an effective prevention strategy in practice.

source_name: Shakhova et al. — Evolution of Approaches to Primary Prevention of Food Allergy: Elimination to Early Introduction (Current Pediatrics 2025)
text: Food allergy in a child is associated with elevated parental anxiety and stress and can affect the mother's psychological wellbeing and the mother-child bond, part of the broader motivation for finding prevention strategies that are actually evidence-based rather than restrictive without proven benefit.

source_name: Shakhova et al. — Evolution of Approaches to Primary Prevention of Food Allergy: Elimination to Early Introduction (Current Pediatrics 2025)
text: Food allergy development is understood as an interaction between genetic predisposition and environmental factors, with nutrition and the microbiome acting as strong epigenetic modulators capable of influencing immune tolerance programming during critical early developmental windows — the underlying rationale for why maternal and infant diet are considered modifiable, high-value prevention targets.

source_name: Shakhova et al. — Evolution of Approaches to Primary Prevention of Food Allergy: Elimination to Early Introduction (Current Pediatrics 2025)
text: Consistent with findings discussed in the APAPARI Asian-perspective literature, some Asian birth cohorts have found low overall food allergy rates despite late allergen introduction, which the Russian review cites as a reason to be cautious about assuming Western early-introduction trial results generalize identically to every population and dietary context.

source_name: Halken et al. — EAACI Guideline: Preventing the Development of Food Allergy in Infants and Young Children (2020 update, Pediatr Allergy Immunol 2021)
text: The EAACI Task Force suggests introducing well-cooked hen's egg — but not raw egg or uncooked pasteurized egg — into the infant diet as part of complementary feeding, to help prevent egg allergy; this is a conditional recommendation based on moderate certainty of evidence.

source_name: Halken et al. — EAACI Guideline: Preventing the Development of Food Allergy in Infants and Young Children (2020 update, Pediatr Allergy Immunol 2021)
text: The recommended amount is based on a trial in which eating at least 2 grams of egg white protein per week (roughly half a well-cooked small egg, twice a week) prevented egg allergy; equivalent amounts of egg baked into other foods are considered appropriate too.

source_name: Halken et al. — EAACI Guideline: Preventing the Development of Food Allergy in Infants and Young Children (2020 update, Pediatr Allergy Immunol 2021)
text: In populations where peanut allergy is prevalent, the EAACI Task Force suggests introducing peanut in an age-appropriate form as part of complementary feeding to help prevent peanut allergy, most effectively from around 4-6 months of life; this is a conditional recommendation based on moderate certainty of evidence, and does not apply as a strong universal rule in countries with low peanut allergy prevalence.

source_name: Halken et al. — EAACI Guideline: Preventing the Development of Food Allergy in Infants and Young Children (2020 update, Pediatr Allergy Immunol 2021)
text: The peanut dose reflected in the evidence is around 2 grams of peanut protein per week, for example one heaped teaspoon of diluted peanut butter; peanut should not be the first solid food given.

source_name: Halken et al. — EAACI Guideline: Preventing the Development of Food Allergy in Infants and Young Children (2020 update, Pediatr Allergy Immunol 2021)
text: The EAACI Task Force suggests against restricting consumption of potential food allergens during pregnancy or breastfeeding to prevent food allergy — the certainty of evidence is very low, but the majority of trials found no reduction in food allergy from maternal avoidance, and unnecessary dietary restriction may reduce intake of important nutrients.

source_name: Halken et al. — EAACI Guideline: Preventing the Development of Food Allergy in Infants and Young Children (2020 update, Pediatr Allergy Immunol 2021)
text: The EAACI Task Force suggests avoiding supplementing breastfed infants with regular cow's milk formula in the first week of life, based on low-certainty evidence that this supplementation may increase the risk of cow's milk allergy; most healthy, mature breastfed infants do not need supplementation in this window.

source_name: Halken et al. — EAACI Guideline: Preventing the Development of Food Allergy in Infants and Young Children (2020 update, Pediatr Allergy Immunol 2021)
text: The EAACI Task Force suggests against introducing soy protein-based formula in the first 6 months of life to prevent cow's milk allergy — evidence of benefit is very low certainty, and there are theoretical concerns about phytate, aluminium, and phyto-oestrogen content at that age.

source_name: Halken et al. — EAACI Guideline: Preventing the Development of Food Allergy in Infants and Young Children (2020 update, Pediatr Allergy Immunol 2021)
text: The EAACI Task Force suggests against using BCG vaccination specifically as a food allergy prevention measure — evidence of any allergy-preventive effect is low certainty and inconsistent; this is separate from BCG's established role in tuberculosis prevention, which families should still follow per their national immunization schedule.

source_name: Halken et al. — EAACI Guideline: Preventing the Development of Food Allergy in Infants and Young Children (2020 update, Pediatr Allergy Immunol 2021)
text: EAACI makes no recommendation for or against breastfeeding specifically as a food allergy prevention strategy, because the evidence (from observational studies only, since RCTs of breastfeeding are not ethical) is very low certainty; however, breastfeeding continues to be encouraged for its many other well-established benefits to infant and maternal health.

source_name: Halken et al. — EAACI Guideline: Preventing the Development of Food Allergy in Infants and Young Children (2020 update, Pediatr Allergy Immunol 2021)
text: EAACI makes no recommendation for or against partially or extensively hydrolyzed formula for preventing cow's milk allergy — evidence is low certainty, with no consistent proof that hydrolyzed formula reduces allergy risk compared with standard formula, nor consistent evidence it causes harm.

source_name: Halken et al. — EAACI Guideline: Preventing the Development of Food Allergy in Infants and Young Children (2020 update, Pediatr Allergy Immunol 2021)
text: EAACI makes no recommendation for or against vitamin or fish oil supplementation in pregnant/breastfeeding women or infants specifically for food allergy prevention; evidence on vitamins was very low certainty, and on fish oil was low certainty, with a possible slight benefit only in infants at increased hereditary risk when fish oil was taken through pregnancy and continued during breastfeeding.

source_name: Halken et al. — EAACI Guideline: Preventing the Development of Food Allergy in Infants and Young Children (2020 update, Pediatr Allergy Immunol 2021)
text: EAACI makes no recommendation for or against prebiotics, probiotics, or synbiotics for mothers or infants for food allergy prevention; evidence is very low certainty, and effects of one specific probiotic strain or combination cannot be assumed to apply to others, since they are immunologically distinct.

source_name: Halken et al. — EAACI Guideline: Preventing the Development of Food Allergy in Infants and Young Children (2020 update, Pediatr Allergy Immunol 2021)
text: EAACI makes no recommendation for or against using emollients as a skin barrier to prevent food allergy; the trial reviewed found little to no effect, and a further trial (BEEP) published after the systematic review also found daily emollient did not reduce eczema or allergy risk at 2 years in high-risk infants.

source_name: Halken et al. — EAACI Guideline: Preventing the Development of Food Allergy in Infants and Young Children (2020 update, Pediatr Allergy Immunol 2021)
text: EAACI makes no recommendation for or against preventive oral immunotherapy (e.g., house dust mite oral immunotherapy) to prevent food allergy in infants who have not yet developed one — the one relevant trial reviewed gave very low-certainty evidence of little to no effect.

source_name: Halken et al. — EAACI Guideline: Preventing the Development of Food Allergy in Infants and Young Children (2020 update, Pediatr Allergy Immunol 2021)
text: All EAACI recommendations in this guideline apply to infants up to 1 year and young children up to 5 years, regardless of their baseline risk of allergy, and are intended for infants who have not yet developed a food allergy; children with symptoms suggestive of existing food allergy should be referred to a specialist allergy service rather than managed under these prevention recommendations.

source_name: Halken et al. — EAACI Guideline: Preventing the Development of Food Allergy in Infants and Young Children (2020 update, Pediatr Allergy Immunol 2021)
text: Recommendations are graded using the GRADE approach: 'the Task Force recommends' denotes a strong recommendation appropriate for most people, while 'the Task Force suggests' denotes a conditional recommendation, meaning many people should be offered it but individual circumstances and preferences may lead clinicians to a different choice with some families.

source_name: Halken et al. — EAACI Guideline: Preventing the Development of Food Allergy in Infants and Young Children (2020 update, Pediatr Allergy Immunol 2021)
text: All EAACI recommendations were agreed by full task force consensus except the strength of the peanut-timing recommendation, where 72% of voting members favored a conditional recommendation and 28% favored a strong recommendation; the conditional wording was ultimately adopted.

source_name: Halken et al. — EAACI Guideline: Preventing the Development of Food Allergy in Infants and Young Children (2020 update, Pediatr Allergy Immunol 2021)
text: The guideline explicitly lists priority research gaps, including confirmatory evidence on peanut introduction outside the UK, the ideal amount and timing of cow's milk protein introduction, and whether infant/maternal diet diversity affects allergy development — areas the Task Force flags as needing further high-quality trials rather than settled questions.

source_name: Halken et al. — EAACI Guideline: Preventing the Development of Food Allergy in Infants and Young Children (2020 update, Pediatr Allergy Immunol 2021)
text: This guideline does not include a specific recommendation or corrected-age adjustment for premature infants; its recommendations are stated generally for infants up to 1 year and young children up to 5 years, without a stated premature-infant subgroup analysis.

source_name: Halken et al. — EAACI Guideline: Preventing the Development of Food Allergy in Infants and Young Children (2020 update, Pediatr Allergy Immunol 2021)
text: EAACI stated its intention to update this guideline again around 2026 unless significant new evidence emerged sooner, treating it as a living, periodically revised guideline rather than a fixed final statement.

source_name: ESPGHAN Committee on Nutrition: Complementary Feeding Position Paper
text: Exclusive or full breastfeeding should be promoted for at least 4 months (17 weeks), with exclusive/predominant breastfeeding to about 6 months considered a desirable goal.

source_name: ESPGHAN Committee on Nutrition: Complementary Feeding Position Paper
text: Complementary foods should not be introduced before 4 months of age but should not be delayed beyond 6 months.

source_name: ESPGHAN Committee on Nutrition: Complementary Feeding Position Paper
text: Gastrointestinal and renal function are sufficiently mature by approximately 4 months to process complementary foods; motor skills to safely manage complementary foods are attained by 4-6 months.

source_name: ESPGHAN Committee on Nutrition: Complementary Feeding Position Paper
text: Allergenic foods may be introduced any time from 4 months (17 weeks) once complementary feeding is commenced.

source_name: ESPGHAN Committee on Nutrition: Complementary Feeding Position Paper
text: Infants at high risk of peanut allergy (severe eczema, egg allergy, or both, as defined in the LEAP study) should have peanut (e.g., as smooth peanut butter) introduced between 4 and 11 months, following evaluation by an appropriately trained professional.

source_name: ESPGHAN Committee on Nutrition: Complementary Feeding Position Paper
text: There may be an increased risk of allergy if solids are introduced before 3-4 months, but there is no evidence that delaying allergenic food introduction beyond 4 months reduces allergy risk, in the general population or those with family history of atopy.

source_name: ESPGHAN Committee on Nutrition: Complementary Feeding Position Paper
text: A systematic review/meta-analysis found moderate-certainty evidence that early egg introduction (4-6 months) was associated with reduced egg allergy risk (RR 0.56), consistent across normal-, high-, and very-high-risk populations.

source_name: ESPGHAN Committee on Nutrition: Complementary Feeding Position Paper
text: Moderate-certainty evidence from 2 trials (EAT and LEAP) showed early peanut introduction (4-11 months) was associated with reduced peanut allergy risk (RR 0.29).

source_name: ESPGHAN Committee on Nutrition: Complementary Feeding Position Paper
text: New foods, including commonly allergenic foods, can be introduced on successive days with no evidence of harm from this approach.

source_name: ESPGHAN Committee on Nutrition: Complementary Feeding Position Paper
text: Prolonged use of pureed foods should be discouraged; infants should be eating lumpy foods by 8-10 months at the latest, with timely progression to finger foods and self-feeding.

source_name: ESPGHAN Committee on Nutrition: Complementary Feeding Position Paper
text: Whole cow's milk should not be used as the main drink before 12 months of age.

source_name: ESPGHAN Committee on Nutrition: Complementary Feeding Position Paper
text: All infants should receive iron-rich complementary foods, including meat products and/or iron-fortified foods.

source_name: ESPGHAN Committee on Nutrition: Complementary Feeding Position Paper
text: No sugar or salt should be added to complementary foods; fruit juices and sugar-sweetened beverages should be avoided.

source_name: ESPGHAN Committee on Nutrition: Complementary Feeding Position Paper
text: Gluten may be introduced between 4 and 12 months of age; large quantities should be avoided in the first weeks after introduction and during infancy.

source_name: ESPGHAN Committee on Nutrition: Complementary Feeding Position Paper
text: Honey should not be introduced before 12 months of age due to association with infant botulism.

source_name: ESPGHAN Committee on Nutrition: Complementary Feeding Position Paper
text: Vegan diets should only be used under appropriate medical or dietetic supervision; failing to follow supplementation advice can cause severe/irreversible consequences including cognitive impairment.

source_name: ESPGHAN/EAP/ESPR/EAACI et al.: Multisociety Response to WHO Complementary Feeding Guideline
text: WHO's 2023 guideline recommends complementary foods be introduced at 6 months (180 days) while continuing to breastfeed (strong, low-certainty evidence).

source_name: ESPGHAN/EAP/ESPR/EAACI et al.: Multisociety Response to WHO Complementary Feeding Guideline
text: The responding societies note WHO's guideline does not address the appropriate age for introduction of allergenic foods, despite rising global burden of childhood allergic disease.

source_name: ESPGHAN/EAP/ESPR/EAACI et al.: Multisociety Response to WHO Complementary Feeding Guideline
text: The multisociety response states that high-quality RCT evidence shows earlier introduction of allergenic complementary foods before 6 months, with continued breastfeeding, can markedly reduce food allergy risk - contradicting WHO's silence on allergen timing.

source_name: ESPGHAN/EAP/ESPR/EAACI et al.: Multisociety Response to WHO Complementary Feeding Guideline
text: The societies cite a European evidence-based guideline concluding the most effective window for introducing peanut for allergy risk reduction is 4-6 months of age - suggesting WHO's single 6-month recommendation may be suboptimal for allergy prevention.

source_name: ESPGHAN/EAP/ESPR/EAACI et al.: Multisociety Response to WHO Complementary Feeding Guideline
text: The societies' suggested alternative: in populations affected by food allergy, complementary foods with high allergenic potential (e.g., well-cooked egg or peanut) may be introduced in age-appropriate form any time from 4 months.

source_name: ESPGHAN/EAP/ESPR/EAACI et al.: Multisociety Response to WHO Complementary Feeding Guideline
text: Randomized trial evidence shows introducing complementary foods at about 4-6 months did not reduce the rate or duration of subsequent breastfeeding compared to later introduction.

source_name: ESPGHAN/EAP/ESPR/EAACI et al.: Multisociety Response to WHO Complementary Feeding Guideline
text: The societies note WHO's rationale for developmental readiness (ability to sit without support) is not evidence-based and applies to finger foods, not pureed/mashed foods; no demonstrated link exists between gut/kidney maturity and neurodevelopmental readiness.

source_name: ESPGHAN/EAP/ESPR/EAACI et al.: Multisociety Response to WHO Complementary Feeding Guideline
text: WHO's guideline recommends continued breastfeeding to 2 years or beyond (strong, very-low-certainty evidence); the responding societies disagree with this strong recommendation given evidence of worse outcomes (higher odds of underweight, wasting, dental caries) associated with continued breastfeeding in the systematic review WHO itself commissioned.

source_name: ESPGHAN/EAP/ESPR/EAACI et al.: Multisociety Response to WHO Complementary Feeding Guideline
text: WHO recommends animal milk (not formula) for young children 12-23 months; the societies flag this could unintentionally increase risk of overweight/obesity and double-burden malnutrition due to excess protein intake from cow's milk, and propose context-specific alternatives instead.
