source_name: NIAID Addendum Guidelines for the Prevention of Peanut Allergy in the United States
text: Addendum Guideline 1: Infants with severe eczema, egg allergy, or both should have age-appropriate peanut-containing food introduced as early as 4-6 months to reduce peanut allergy risk; other solids should be introduced first to confirm developmental readiness.

source_name: NIAID Addendum Guidelines for the Prevention of Peanut Allergy in the United States
text: Addendum Guideline 2: Infants with mild-to-moderate eczema should have age-appropriate peanut-containing food introduced around 6 months, in accordance with family preference/culture; dietary peanut can be introduced at home without in-office evaluation.

source_name: NIAID Addendum Guidelines for the Prevention of Peanut Allergy in the United States
text: Addendum Guideline 3: Infants without eczema or any food allergy should have age-appropriate peanut-containing foods freely introduced with other solids, per family preference and cultural practice.

source_name: NIAID Addendum Guidelines for the Prevention of Peanut Allergy in the United States
text: Evaluation with peanut-specific IgE measurement, skin prick testing, or both should be strongly considered before peanut introduction in infants with severe eczema and/or egg allergy, to determine if and how peanut should be introduced.

source_name: NIAID Addendum Guidelines for the Prevention of Peanut Allergy in the United States
text: A peanut sIgE level below 0.35 kUA/L has strong negative predictive value for peanut allergy; a level of 0.35 kUA/L or greater lacks adequate positive predictive value and warrants specialist referral.

source_name: NIAID Addendum Guidelines for the Prevention of Peanut Allergy in the United States
text: Skin prick test wheal diameter categorizes infants: 0-2mm = low risk (introduce at home or supervised), 3-7mm = moderate-to-high risk (supervised feeding or graded oral food challenge), 8mm+ = high likelihood of established allergy (specialist management, avoid).

source_name: NIAID Addendum Guidelines for the Prevention of Peanut Allergy in the United States
text: If peanut introduction is indicated, the cumulative first dose should be approximately 2g of peanut protein; total weekly consumption should be approximately 6-7g over 3 or more feedings.

source_name: NIAID Addendum Guidelines for the Prevention of Peanut Allergy in the United States
text: In the LEAP trial, among infants with negative baseline skin test, peanut allergy prevalence at 60 months was 13.7% in the avoidance group vs 1.9% in the consumption group (86.1% relative risk reduction).

source_name: NIAID Addendum Guidelines for the Prevention of Peanut Allergy in the United States
text: Among LEAP participants with a measurable peanut skin test response at entry, peanut allergy prevalence was 35.3% in the avoidance group vs 10.6% in the consumption group (70% relative risk reduction).

source_name: NIAID Addendum Guidelines for the Prevention of Peanut Allergy in the United States
text: The LEAP-On study demonstrated that benefits achieved in LEAP persisted even after peanut consumers avoided peanut for 1 year (60-72 months), indicating durable oral tolerance.

source_name: NIAID Addendum Guidelines for the Prevention of Peanut Allergy in the United States
text: Introduction of peanut did not affect duration or frequency of breastfeeding and did not influence growth or nutrition, based on nutrition analysis of the LEAP cohort.

source_name: NIAID Addendum Guidelines for the Prevention of Peanut Allergy in the United States
text: For infants identified as allergic to peanut (failed supervised feeding/OFC, or SPT Category C confirmed allergic), strict peanut avoidance is recommended with long-term specialist management.

source_name: NIAID Addendum Guidelines for the Prevention of Peanut Allergy in the United States
text: Whole nuts should not be given to children under 5 years of age; peanut butter directly from a spoon or in lumps/dollops should not be given to children under 4 years due to choking risk.

source_name: Abrams et al.: Updates in Food Allergy Prevention in Children (Pediatrics/AAP)
text: Despite peanut introduction in the first year of life increasing more than threefold in Australia (21.6% to 85.6%, 2007-2018), there was only a nonsignificant decrease in population peanut allergy prevalence (3.1% to 2.6%), suggesting early introduction alone is not sufficient.

source_name: Abrams et al.: Updates in Food Allergy Prevention in Children (Pediatrics/AAP)
text: Regularity of ingestion after introduction appears important: in the PETIT egg-allergy-prevention trial, infants required to eat heated egg powder at least daily showed such a strong protective effect (8% vs 38% egg allergy) that the trial was halted early.

source_name: Abrams et al.: Updates in Food Allergy Prevention in Children (Pediatrics/AAP)
text: In the LEAP study, infants in the early-introduction group ate peanut at least 3 times per week (6g/week) until 5 years of age.

source_name: Abrams et al.: Updates in Food Allergy Prevention in Children (Pediatrics/AAP)
text: The Canadian Society of Allergy and Clinical Immunology (CSACI) recommends both early introduction AND regular ingestion of age-appropriate allergen amounts multiple times per month (goal: at least weekly) for food allergy prevention.

source_name: Abrams et al.: Updates in Food Allergy Prevention in Children (Pediatrics/AAP)
text: The form in which egg is introduced affects allergenicity: raw/pasteurized powdered egg (used in 4 of 5 major RCTs) showed no significant protective effect and/or safety concerns, while gently heated/cooked egg (used in the effective PETIT trial) showed strong protection.

source_name: Abrams et al.: Updates in Food Allergy Prevention in Children (Pediatrics/AAP)
text: A 2010 population-based study found first exposure to cooked egg (stove-cooked) reduced egg allergy risk compared to first exposure via baked goods (OR 0.2).

source_name: Abrams et al.: Updates in Food Allergy Prevention in Children (Pediatrics/AAP)
text: International guidelines disagree on preemptive allergy screening before peanut introduction: NIAID (2017) and the AAP (2019) recommend strongly considering skin prick/IgE testing for high-risk infants, while ASCIA, BSACI, AAAAI/ACAAI, and CSACI explicitly do NOT recommend routine preemptive screening for any risk level.

source_name: Abrams et al.: Updates in Food Allergy Prevention in Children (Pediatrics/AAP)
text: Specificity of skin prick testing and peanut-specific IgE testing is under 50%, meaning most infants with positive tests can actually tolerate the food - screening risks substantial overdiagnosis.

source_name: Abrams et al.: Updates in Food Allergy Prevention in Children (Pediatrics/AAP)
text: The HealthNuts population cohort study found that screening all infants with early-onset eczema and/or egg allergy would require testing 16% of the population and would still miss 23% of peanut allergy cases.

source_name: Abrams et al.: Updates in Food Allergy Prevention in Children (Pediatrics/AAP)
text: There has never been a fatality on first ingestion of a food in infancy, even in high-risk infants; in LEAP, only 2.2% of early-introduction infants had a positive oral food challenge at baseline, with predominantly cutaneous symptoms and no epinephrine required.

source_name: Abrams et al.: Updates in Food Allergy Prevention in Children (Pediatrics/AAP)
text: Practical caregiver guidance: do not rub allergenic food on the infant's skin before feeding; food allergy reactions typically occur within 1-2 hours of ingestion, usually as hives, swelling, or vomiting.

source_name: ESPGHAN Committee on Nutrition: Complementary Feeding Position Paper
text: Continued breastfeeding is recommended alongside complementary feeding; attempts to devise separate recommendations for breast-fed vs formula-fed infants are likely to cause confusion and are not recommended.

source_name: ESPGHAN Committee on Nutrition: Complementary Feeding Position Paper
text: Iron requirements are high during complementary feeding; there is a need for iron-rich foods, particularly for breastfed infants, since endogenous iron stores are used up by around 6 months.

source_name: ESPGHAN Committee on Nutrition: Complementary Feeding Position Paper
text: A high protein intake during complementary feeding may increase risk of subsequent overweight/obesity, especially in predisposed individuals; mean protein energy percentage should not exceed 15%.

source_name: ESPGHAN Committee on Nutrition: Complementary Feeding Position Paper
text: Systematic review evidence found no consistent association between the amount of dietary fat (6-24 months) and later health outcomes; relatively high-fat diets do not appear harmful.

source_name: ESPGHAN Committee on Nutrition: Complementary Feeding Position Paper
text: Data are insufficient to make specific recommendations for choices or composition of complementary feeding based on cognitive or cardiovascular outcomes.

source_name: ESPGHAN Committee on Nutrition: Complementary Feeding Position Paper
text: Infants have innate preferences for sweet and salty tastes and an innate dislike of bitter taste; these predispositions can be modified by early and repeated experience with a food.

source_name: ESPGHAN Committee on Nutrition: Complementary Feeding Position Paper
text: An infant may need to receive a new flavour 8 to 10 times before accepting it; parents should be encouraged to persist in offering a new food even if the infant's facial expression suggests dislike.

source_name: ESPGHAN Committee on Nutrition: Complementary Feeding Position Paper
text: There is currently insufficient evidence to draw conclusions about the most appropriate feeding method (spoon-feeding vs self-feeding/baby-led weaning); parents should be encouraged toward responsive feeding and recognizing hunger/satiety cues.

source_name: ESPGHAN Committee on Nutrition: Complementary Feeding Position Paper
text: Fennel oil and fennel tea preparations are not recommended in children younger than 4 years due to lack of adequate safety data and presence of a naturally occurring genotoxic carcinogen (estragole).

source_name: ESPGHAN Committee on Nutrition: Complementary Feeding Position Paper
text: To reduce exposure to inorganic arsenic (a first-level carcinogen), the ESPGHAN Committee on Nutrition previously recommended that rice drinks should not be used for infants and young children.

source_name: ESPGHAN Committee on Nutrition: Complementary Feeding Position Paper
text: Systematic review evidence found the age of gluten introduction affects incidence of celiac disease autoimmunity in the first 2 years but does not affect cumulative childhood prevalence of celiac disease.

source_name: ESPGHAN Committee on Nutrition: Complementary Feeding Position Paper
text: Neither any breastfeeding nor breastfeeding specifically during gluten introduction has been shown to reduce risk of celiac disease.

source_name: ESPGHAN Committee on Nutrition: Complementary Feeding Position Paper
text: In children at high risk of type 1 diabetes, gluten introduction before 3 months of age was associated with increased risk of type 1 diabetes autoimmunity, but beyond 3 months, age of gluten introduction had no effect on risk.

source_name: ESPGHAN Committee on Nutrition: Complementary Feeding Position Paper
text: Vegan diets during complementary feeding require regular medical/dietetic supervision to ensure sufficient vitamin B12, vitamin D, iron, zinc, folate, n-3 LCPUFA, protein, and calcium.

source_name: ESPGHAN/EAP/ESPR/EAACI et al.: Multisociety Response to WHO Complementary Feeding Guideline
text: The responding societies note there was apparently no wider stakeholder involvement or open public consultation process in developing the WHO 2023 guideline, which they consider essential public-body practice.

source_name: ESPGHAN/EAP/ESPR/EAACI et al.: Multisociety Response to WHO Complementary Feeding Guideline
text: The societies note the WHO guideline development process had contradictory statements about the consensus threshold: one part states 70% approval was needed for all recommendations, another states consensus was used except for nutrient-supplement/fortified-food recommendations which required 70% agreement.

source_name: ESPGHAN/EAP/ESPR/EAACI et al.: Multisociety Response to WHO Complementary Feeding Guideline
text: The societies note the WHO systematic reviews underpinning the guideline considered evidence only up to end of 2020/early 2021 and question why these were not updated before the 2023-2024 publication.

source_name: ESPGHAN/EAP/ESPR/EAACI et al.: Multisociety Response to WHO Complementary Feeding Guideline
text: The societies state that WHO's cited evidence for continued breastfeeding reducing acute gastroenteritis risk in the second year was based on only 1 study (not 2 as WHO stated), which was rated at serious risk of bias.

source_name: ESPGHAN/EAP/ESPR/EAACI et al.: Multisociety Response to WHO Complementary Feeding Guideline
text: The societies criticize WHO's guideline for not considering the very common high-income-country scenario of infants receiving infant formula alongside complementary foods when modeling nutritional adequacy (via Optifood).

source_name: ESPGHAN/EAP/ESPR/EAACI et al.: Multisociety Response to WHO Complementary Feeding Guideline
text: The societies clarify that the ESPGHAN position paper on Young Child Formulas does NOT state these formulas are unnecessary (as WHO's guideline implies via apparent mis-citation), but rather that there is no necessity for their ROUTINE use in ages 1-3 years, while noting they can serve a targeted nutritional strategy.

source_name: NIAID Addendum Guidelines for the Prevention of Peanut Allergy in the United States
text: The NIAID panel does not recommend food allergen panel testing or sIgE testing for foods other than peanut, due to poor positive predictive value, risk of food-allergy misinterpretation/overdiagnosis, and unnecessary dietary restriction.

source_name: NIAID Addendum Guidelines for the Prevention of Peanut Allergy in the United States
text: SPT reagents, testing devices, and methodology can differ significantly among US health care providers; specialists should adjust SPT categorization criteria to their own training and experience.

source_name: NIAID Addendum Guidelines for the Prevention of Peanut Allergy in the United States
text: In the HealthNuts study, a peanut SPT wheal diameter of 8mm or greater had a 95% positive predictive value for peanut allergy (positive oral food challenge result).

source_name: NIAID Addendum Guidelines for the Prevention of Peanut Allergy in the United States
text: Caregivers of infants eligible for early peanut introduction who have older siblings or caregivers with established peanut allergy should discuss with their health care provider the benefit (reduced risk to the infant) versus risk (potential further sensitization/accidental exposure to the allergic family member) of adding peanut to the infant's diet.

source_name: NIAID Addendum Guidelines for the Prevention of Peanut Allergy in the United States
text: Recipe options for delivering approximately 2g of peanut protein at home include: ~21 pieces of Bamba peanut puff softened with water, 2 teaspoons of thinned smooth peanut butter, 2 teaspoons of peanut butter mixed with pureed fruit/vegetable, or 2 teaspoons of peanut flour or peanut butter powder mixed with pureed fruit/vegetable.

source_name: NIAID Addendum Guidelines for the Prevention of Peanut Allergy in the United States
text: Home feeding instructions specify: feed only when the infant is healthy (no cold, vomiting, diarrhea, or other illness); give the first peanut feeding at home, not at daycare or a restaurant; ensure an adult can give full attention and observe the infant for at least 2 hours afterward for signs of allergic reaction.

source_name: NIAID Addendum Guidelines for the Prevention of Peanut Allergy in the United States
text: Mild allergic reaction symptoms include a new rash or a few hives around the mouth/face; more severe symptoms include lip/face/tongue swelling, vomiting, widespread hives, difficulty breathing, wheeze, repetitive coughing, change in skin color, or sudden lethargy - any of which warrant immediate medical attention.

source_name: NIAID Addendum Guidelines for the Prevention of Peanut Allergy in the United States
text: The 2017 Addendum's quality-of-evidence rating for Guideline 1 (severe eczema/egg allergy infants) is Moderate, derived primarily from the single randomized, open-label LEAP trial, though bolstered by double-blind placebo-controlled assessment of the primary outcome and supporting epidemiologic data from Israel.

source_name: NIAID Addendum Guidelines for the Prevention of Peanut Allergy in the United States
text: The quality-of-evidence rating for Guideline 2 (mild-to-moderate eczema) is Low, since it is based on extrapolation of data from a single study population that the original LEAP trial did not specifically target.

source_name: NIAID Addendum Guidelines for the Prevention of Peanut Allergy in the United States
text: The quality-of-evidence rating for Guideline 3 (no eczema/food allergy) is Low; the panel acknowledges any benefit/harm analysis in this population relies primarily on expert opinion given current differences in regional peanut consumption and sensitization rates.

source_name: NIAID Addendum Guidelines for the Prevention of Peanut Allergy in the United States
text: Approximately 14% of all children with peanut allergy at age 12-18 months in the HealthNuts Study lacked known risk factors for food allergy, meaning low-risk infants still contribute substantially to the overall societal burden of peanut allergy.

source_name: NIAID Addendum Guidelines for the Prevention of Peanut Allergy in the United States
text: Severe eczema is defined as persistent or frequently recurring eczema with typical morphology/distribution, assessed as severe by a health care provider, requiring frequent prescription-strength topical corticosteroids, calcineurin inhibitors, or other anti-inflammatory agents despite appropriate emollient use.

source_name: NIAID Addendum Guidelines for the Prevention of Peanut Allergy in the United States
text: Egg allergy, for purposes of this addendum, is defined as a history of an allergic reaction to egg plus a skin prick test wheal diameter of 3mm or greater with egg white extract, or a positive oral egg food challenge result.

source_name: Abrams et al.: Updates in Food Allergy Prevention in Children (Pediatrics/AAP)
text: Delayed (after 14 days) and/or irregular (less than once daily) cow's milk ingestion significantly increased risk of cow's milk allergy compared to introduction in the first 14 days with regular daily exposure thereafter (OR 19.3) in a prospective study of over 13,000 infants.

source_name: Abrams et al.: Updates in Food Allergy Prevention in Children (Pediatrics/AAP)
text: A follow-up study of siblings of peanut-allergic children found the risk of developing peanut allergy was 0% among those eating peanut at least monthly, 3% among those eating it less than monthly, and 18% among those who had stopped eating peanut entirely.

source_name: Abrams et al.: Updates in Food Allergy Prevention in Children (Pediatrics/AAP)
text: The bulk of RCT evidence for benefit of early allergenic solid introduction exists specifically for peanut, egg, and cow's milk; there are no RCTs focused exclusively on tree nut, soy, grains, seeds, legumes, finfish, or shellfish.

source_name: Abrams et al.: Updates in Food Allergy Prevention in Children (Pediatrics/AAP)
text: There is no evidence of harm from early feeding of common allergens other than peanut/egg/milk, and the mechanism of sensitization is thought to be similar across all common allergens.

source_name: Abrams et al.: Updates in Food Allergy Prevention in Children (Pediatrics/AAP)
text: AAAAI/ACAAI/CSACI joint guidance states there is insufficient evidence to support a precise dose and frequency necessary to support tolerance, recommending simply feeding age-appropriate amounts the child enjoys with regular frequency - a less prescriptive stance than NIAID's specific 6-7g/week peanut protein target.

source_name: Abrams et al.: Updates in Food Allergy Prevention in Children (Pediatrics/AAP)
text: Commercial multi-allergen infant food products (powders, puffs, cereals, cookies) marketed since the NIAID addendum show significant inter- and intra-product variability in protein content per allergen, and none have direct evidence demonstrating they prevent food allergy development.

source_name: Abrams et al.: Updates in Food Allergy Prevention in Children (Pediatrics/AAP)
text: Only 31% of surveyed soon-to-be or current parents were willing to introduce peanut before 6 months of age, one year after the NIAID addendum guidelines were published - indicating a significant caregiver acceptance gap.

source_name: BSACI/FASG Guidance on Early Introduction of Food Allergens
text: For healthy infants, exclusive breastfeeding is advised for the first 6 months, with complementary foods introduced from around 6 months (not before 4 months). Egg and peanut should not be excluded from an infant's diet once solids start, and should be introduced before age one if part of the family's diet.

source_name: BSACI/FASG Guidance on Early Introduction of Food Allergens (higher-risk infants)
text: Infants considered higher risk (moderate-to-severe eczema, or eczema starting in the first 3 months of life) may benefit from earlier introduction of egg and then peanut, starting from 4 months once solids have begun, in an age-appropriate form to avoid choking.

source_name: BSACI/FASG Guidance - family history clarification
text: Having another family member with a food allergy does not by itself put an infant in the higher-risk category. What matters more is how introduction is managed safely around an already food-allergic person in the household. BSACI recommends parents of infants with pre-existing food allergy or severe eczema get individual advice from a healthcare professional.

source_name: BSACI/FASG Guidance - allergen sequencing
text: Evidence points to a possible window of opportunity where egg is introduced ahead of peanut, with other allergens following once the infant is established on solid foods such as pureed fruit and vegetables.

source_name: BSACI/FASG Guidance - testing and supervised introduction
text: BSACI does not recommend routine allergy testing before introducing egg or peanut in higher-risk infants, since limited UK testing access can cause delays that themselves raise allergy risk. Testing is only advised where a rapid, specialist-supervised food challenge is available to confirm a true allergy; otherwise families are guided to introduce allergens gradually at home.

source_name: BSACI/FASG Guidance - reaction management
text: Families should be supported to tell mild irritant reactions apart from true allergic reactions, and be equipped to manage mild reactions at home while knowing when to escalate to medical care. If an actual food allergy is suspected during introduction, BSACI advises stopping that food and seeking medical advice.

source_name: CPS: Timing of Introduction of Allergenic Solids for Infants at High Risk
text: For infants at high risk of allergic disease, CPS recommends introducing commonly allergenic solids at around 6 months, but not before 4 months, guided by the infant's developmental readiness rather than a fixed calendar date.

source_name: CPS/CSACI Joint Statement - Dietary Exposures and Allergy Prevention in High-Risk Infants
text: CPS states there is strong evidence that introducing allergenic foods early (around 6 months, not before 4 months) helps prevent common food allergies in high-risk infants, particularly to peanut and egg.

source_name: CPS/CSACI Joint Statement - maintaining tolerance
text: Once cow's milk protein formula or another allergenic food is introduced, CPS advises keeping up regular ingestion of that food (as little as roughly 10 mL daily for milk) to avoid the infant losing tolerance they've built.

source_name: Food Allergy Canada (CPS/CSACI-sourced) - introducing allergens practically
text: CPS guidance recommends actively offering non-choking forms of common allergens like peanut and egg around 6 months (not before 4 months). Foods can be introduced one at a time to help identify any reaction, though CPS notes there's no strong evidence this spacing is strictly necessary.

source_name: Food Allergy Canada (CPS/CSACI-sourced) - screening and testing stance
text: Similar to BSACI, CPS/CSACI advise against routine pre-introduction allergy testing due to false-positive risk, and specify testing should only happen where fast access to a supervised food challenge exists to confirm a real allergy.

source_name: CPS - Early Allergenic Food Introduction Guidance (pandemic-era reaffirmation)
text: CPS reaffirms that high-risk infants (eczema, existing food allergy, or immediate family history of allergy) should have allergenic solids introduced early -- around 6 months, not before 4 -- one food at a time, without unnecessary delay between them.

source_name: BSACI - Early introduction of food allergens (live guidance page)
text: BSACI's current guidance names only two higher-risk groups for allergen introduction: babies with eczema, and babies with a pre-existing food allergy. It explicitly states that having another family member in the household with a food allergy does not by itself place an infant in the higher-risk category, though households should still take care in how the allergen is introduced to keep the already-allergic family member safe.

source_name: CPS: Timing of Introduction of Allergenic Solids for Infants at High Risk (risk-definition passage)
text: CPS's practice point defines a high-risk infant as one with either a personal history of atopy (e.g. eczema, an existing food allergy) or a first-degree relative with atopy. This makes family history alone a qualifying criterion for early introduction, in contrast to guidance that treats family history as not raising an infant's risk category on its own.
